442.title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
442.hook: Luke writes to Theophilus, lover of God, so he may know the certainty
442.howItsDone: Catholics hear the Gospel of Luke read through at Sunday Mass every third year (Year C), and Luke's preface is proclaimed on a Sunday in Ordinary Time; his feast day is October 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judas Maccabeus prayed for his fallen soldiers, and we closed fifty days of kings, prophets and wisdom. Your line was a holy and wholesome thought. Whose names did you write down? Day four hundred forty-two, and a new block: the Gospel of Luke.

Most books of the Bible never tell you who wrote them, or why. They just begin. Luke is different. Before a single angel appears, before Bethlehem, there's a short preface, four verses that are one long, polished sentence in Greek, the kind that opened histories and medical treatises in that world. It's the writer stepping out from behind the curtain for a moment and telling you what he's doing. And he isn't writing to the world in general. He's writing to one person, by name.
screen: `MOST BOOKS JUST BEGIN.` → `FOUR VERSES, ONE GREEK SENTENCE.` → `WRITTEN TO ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening in the Douay-Rheims: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a narration of the things that have been accomplished among us." Notice the first thing he says: others have already tried this. Many of them. He's not the first. Then he says where his material came from: from those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning, and ministers of the word. So Luke is not claiming to be an eyewitness himself. He's a careful second-generation writer who has, in his words, diligently traced everything from the start. And then: it seemed good to me also "to write to thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." Theophilus is a Greek name: theos, God, and philos, friend or lover. Friend of God. Was he a real person? Most excellent was a polite title for an official or a person of rank, so he may have been a real patron who paid for the copying. But since early centuries readers have also noticed that anyone who loves God fits the name, and Saint Ambrose said as much. Both can be true. And Theophilus already knows the story; he's been instructed. Luke writes so he can stand on solid ground. The Greek word for verity is asphaleia: firmness, safety, footing that won't slip. Luke wrote a second volume, too, the Acts of the Apostles, also addressed to Theophilus. The Gospel never names its author; early Christian writers name Luke, the companion called the most dear physician in the Letter to the Colossians. For the next fifty days, we'll read his account in order.
screen: `MANY HAVE TAKEN IN HAND.` · `FROM EYEWITNESSES, NOT AN EYEWITNESS.` · `THEOPHILUS: FRIEND OF GOD.` · `ASPHALEIA: SOLID FOOTING.` · then, large: `THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you're certain of. Settle, and breathe. Not everything. Not the whole Creed, unless that's where you are. Just one thing you could stand on if the floor shook. Maybe it's that someone loves you. That a certain kindness was real. That God was there in a particular moment. That truth matters. Let it come, and test it gently: does it hold? Then, after the bell, write it down, the way Luke wrote for Theophilus, so you'll have it on paper. If you pray, you can thank God for that solid ground. The bell holds the time.
Theophilus. Friend of God, the man Luke addressed his careful, orderly account to, drawing on eyewitnesses from the beginning. Today's word.
Your line: written for you. Today, read Luke's first four verses yourself, and put your own name where it says Theophilus. Day four hundred forty-two.

myth: Luke says he was an eyewitness of everything he writes
he says he drew on eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, and traced it all carefully.
Luke addresses Acts to Theophilus too
Acts opens by addressing Theophilus again; the two books are a pair.
the Gospel names Luke as its author in its text
the text never names him; early Christian writers attribute it to Luke, Paul's companion.

fork.setup: you're Luke. many others have already written accounts of Jesus. what do you do?
options: leave it to them.
trace everything carefully from the beginning and write an orderly account for Theophilus.
write a new story with no sources.
fork.reveal: it seemed good to me also, he says, having traced all things from the beginning, to write to thee in order.

original.note: Greek: Theophilus, friend of God or dear to God, from theos and philos.

trapdoor: what you thought: the boring bit before the Christmas story.
what it means: the writer tells you his method: others wrote first, he used eyewitnesses, and he wrote in order so a friend of God could stand on solid ground.
what a scholar hears: one long Greek period in the style of Hellenistic historians; asphaleia, certainty; the same Theophilus in Acts 1:1.

sources.ref: Ambrose, Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, Book 1

443.title: Zachary struck silent (Luke 1:5–25)
443.hook: an old priest doubts the angel and can't speak for nine months
443.howItsDone: Catholics hear the announcement to Zachary at Mass in the days before Christmas and on the vigil of the Nativity of John the Baptist, and some keep silence before the Blessed Sacrament in Eucharistic adoration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's preface: an orderly account for Theophilus, friend of God. Your line was written for you. Did you put your own name in? Day four hundred forty-three.

Luke's story doesn't open in Bethlehem. It opens in the Temple in Jerusalem, with an old couple. Zachary is a priest. His wife Elizabeth comes from a priestly family too. Both of them, Luke says, were just before God, walking blamelessly. And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were well advanced in years. In that world, that was a grief people could see. One day Zachary's division of priests is on duty, and the lot falls on him to go into the sanctuary and burn incense. He goes in alone.
screen: `NOT BETHLEHEM: THE TEMPLE.` → `JUST, BLAMELESS, AND CHILDLESS.` → `THE LOT FALLS ON ZACHARY.`

segments.voice: Outside, the whole crowd is praying at the hour of incense. Inside, alone, Zachary sees an angel standing at the right side of the altar, and he's terrified. The angel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Fear not, Zachary, for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elizabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Thy prayer is heard. Which prayer? Luke doesn't say. Some readers hear the old prayer for a child; others, a priest's prayer for his people. The son will be great, will drink no wine, will be filled with the Holy Ghost, and will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias. And Zachary, a good man, a priest, standing in the holiest room he'll ever stand in, asks for proof: "Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years." The angel answers: I am Gabriel, who stand before God. And because you didn't believe my words, you'll be mute, unable to speak, until the day these things happen. Outside, people are wondering why he's taking so long. He comes out and can't speak to them. He can only make signs, and they realize he's seen a vision. Then he goes home, and Elizabeth conceives. People often say nine months, but it's longer than that: his silence lasts until the baby is born and named. Is it a punishment? It is, the angel says so. But some readers hear something else in it too. A priest whose work was prayers and blessings was given a long season with no words at all, and when his voice comes back, the first thing it does is bless God. We'll hear the song in two days. His name, Zachary, means the Lord has remembered.
screen: `THY PRAYER IS HEARD.` · `WHEREBY SHALL I KNOW THIS?` · `I AM GABRIEL. YOU WILL BE MUTE.` · `A SEASON WITH NO WORDS.` · then, large: `FEAR NOT, ZACHARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin a silence. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, don't talk, even in your head, as much as you can. When words come, let them go past, like people walking by a window. Notice how much of your inner noise is commentary, arguing, planning what to say. Let it quiet down. Then, after the bell, choose one hour today to keep silence: phone face down, no music, no podcasts, as few words as your life allows. If you pray, you can give that hour to God and listen. The bell holds the time.
Zachary. The old priest who asked the angel for proof, and could not speak again until his son John was born and named. Today's word.
Your line: silence taught him. Today, keep your hour of silence, and notice what you hear in it. Day four hundred forty-three.

Gabriel told Zachary his prayer was heard

Luke's Gospel begins in Bethlehem

fork.setup: you're Zachary, an old priest alone at the altar of incense. an angel tells you your elderly wife will bear a son. what do you say?
options: thank God, and go out rejoicing.
ask: how shall I know this? I'm an old man.
say nothing and run out.
fork.reveal: "whereby shall I know this?" he asks for proof, and he gets a sign he didn't want: no words until it's fulfilled.

original.note: Hebrew: Zechariah, the Lord has remembered. in Greek, Zacharias; in the Douay, Zachary.

trapdoor: what you thought: an angel punishes an old man for a question.
what it means: a good priest, at the high point of his life, can't believe his long prayer is answered, and is given a long silence until it comes true.
what a scholar hears: Zechariah means the Lord remembered; priests served in divisions chosen by lot; and the silence ends in the Benedictus.

444.title: Hail, full of grace (Luke 1:26–38)
444.hook: the angel's greeting, Mary's question, and her yes
444.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Hail Mary, whose first half is the angel's greeting and Elizabeth's, in the rosary and the Angelus, and celebrate the Annunciation on March 25; the scene is the first Joyful Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zachary asked the angel for proof and went silent. Your line was silence taught him. What did you hear in your hour of quiet? Day four hundred forty-four.

Six months later, Luke says, the same angel is sent again. But look where. Last time it was the sanctuary of the Temple in Jerusalem, to a priest at the altar of incense. This time it's a town in Galilee called Nazareth, to a young woman espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. No altar. No incense. No crowd outside. Luke gives her name last, as if he's saving it: and the virgin's name was Mary.
screen: `THE SAME ANGEL, SENT AGAIN.` → `NOT THE TEMPLE: NAZARETH.` → `AND THE VIRGIN'S NAME WAS MARY.`

segments.voice: The angel comes in and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail, in Latin, is Ave. The Greek word, chaire, was an ordinary greeting, and it also means rejoice. Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitomene, a form that means something like one who has been graced, and remains so. It's the angel's name for her, almost in place of her name. Catholics hear in it the fullness of grace that marks Mary's whole life; the King James Version has it as highly favored. Mary is troubled, Luke says, and she thinks about what kind of greeting this could be. Fear not, Mary, the angel says, you have found grace with God, and you'll conceive and bear a son and call him Jesus. And then Mary asks a question, just as Zachary did: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" But it's a different kind of question. Zachary asked how he could know. Mary asks how it will happen. Some readers have noticed the difference: one asks for proof, the other for the way. The angel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee. And your kinswoman Elizabeth, the barren one, is in her sixth month, because no word shall be impossible with God. Then her answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, fiat: let it be. And the angel departs. Catholics keep this moment as the feast of the Annunciation.
screen: `AVE: HAIL, AND REJOICE.` · `KECHARITOMENE: GRACED, AND REMAINING SO.` · `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` · `FIAT: BE IT DONE TO ME.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray, or simply hold, the first half of the Hail Mary. Settle, and breathe. Its first half is made of Luke's words, with two names added: the angel's greeting, and then, a few verses on, Elizabeth's. If you pray, say it slowly, one phrase to each breath. Hail Mary, full of grace. The Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women. And blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. If you don't pray it, just sit with the greeting itself, the Lord is with thee, and notice what it would be like to hear it said to you. The bell holds the time.
Ave. Latin for hail, the angel Gabriel's first word to Mary at Nazareth, and the first word of the Hail Mary. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace. Today, when something unexpected is asked of you, try Mary's two steps: ask how, then say yes if you can. Day four hundred forty-four.

myth: Mary asked for a sign the way Zachary did
Zachary asked how he could know; Mary asked how it would be done. some readers have noted the difference.
the first half of the Hail Mary comes from Luke's Gospel

fork.setup: you're Mary in Nazareth. an angel says you will bear a son, though you know not man. what do you say?
options: ask for proof first.
ask how it will be done, and then say: be it done to me according to thy word.
send the angel away.
fork.reveal: she asks how, hears the answer, and says: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."

original.note: Greek: full of grace, highly favored; a form meaning one who has been graced, and remains so.

trapdoor: what you thought: the words of a prayer.
what it means: an angel's greeting to a young woman in a village, her honest question, and her free yes.
what a scholar hears: chaire, a greeting that also means rejoice; kecharitomene, a perfect passive participle used almost as a name; and fiat, Mary's yes in the Latin.

445.title: Zachary's song (Luke 1:57–80)
445.hook: his tongue loosed, he sings of the dayspring from on high, prayed every morning
445.howItsDone: The Benedictus, Zachary's canticle, is prayed every morning at Lauds (Morning Prayer) in the Liturgy of the Hours by priests and religious, and by lay Catholics who pray the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the angel's greeting at Nazareth, and Mary's question and her yes. Your line was full of grace. When were you asked something unexpected? Day four hundred forty-five.

Elizabeth gives birth to a son, and the neighbors and relatives come to rejoice with her. On the eighth day they gather for his circumcision and naming, and they've already decided: he'll be Zachary, after his father. Elizabeth says no. He shall be called John. But nobody in your family has that name, they say. So they turn to the father, still mute after all these months, and make signs: what do you want him called? Zachary asks for a writing tablet. Everyone leans in. And he writes four words: "John is his name."
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY.` → `NOBODY IN YOUR FAMILY IS JOHN.` → `A TABLET, AND FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: And immediately, Luke says, his mouth is opened and his tongue loosed, and he speaks, blessing God. The silence ends with obedience; he names the child the way the angel said. And what comes out of him, filled with the Holy Ghost, is a song. It's called the Benedictus, after its first word in Latin. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; because he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people." The first half looks back: the house of David, the prophets, the oath God swore to Abraham. Then he turns to the baby in front of him. And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest, to go before the face of the Lord and prepare his ways. And then the image the carry comes from. The King James calls it the dayspring: "the dayspring from on high hath visited us." The Douay calls it the Orient: "the Orient from on high hath visited us: To enlighten them that sit in darkness, and in the shadow of death; to direct our feet into the way of peace." Dayspring and Orient are both trying to catch one Greek word, anatole: the rising of the sun, the dawn, the place in the sky where light comes up. Christians hear in it Christ pictured as sunrise, coming to people sitting in the dark. So the Church sets this song at dawn: in the Liturgy of the Hours, the Benedictus is sung every morning at Lauds, Morning Prayer. Months of silence, and the song that broke them became the Church's morning song.
screen: `JOHN IS HIS NAME.` · `BLESSED BE THE LORD GOD OF ISRAEL.` · `ANATOLE: DAYSPRING, ORIENT, DAWN.` · `SUNG EVERY MORNING AT LAUDS.` · then, large: `TO DIRECT OUR FEET INTO THE WAY OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one line for sunrise. Settle, and breathe. Picture tomorrow's first light: the gray before dawn, then a line of gold at the window. From the song, choose one phrase to carry into that moment. The dayspring from on high. To enlighten them that sit in darkness. To direct our feet into the way of peace. Say it over a few times now, slowly, until it's yours. Tomorrow at sunrise, or whenever you first see daylight, say it once. If you pray, it becomes a prayer. If you don't, let it be a way of greeting the light. The bell holds the time.
Benedictus. Latin for blessed, the first word of Zachary's song when his tongue was loosed, prayed by the Church every morning. Today's word.
Your line: the dayspring from on high. Tomorrow at first light, say the line you chose before you say anything else. Day four hundred forty-five.

pairs: where the Church sings it daily

after his father. Elizabeth said John, and Zachary wrote it down.
the Douay and the King James use the same word for the dayspring
the King James has dayspring; the Douay has Orient. both translate anatole, the sunrise.
the Benedictus is prayed only at Christmas

fork.setup: you're Zachary, mute for months. your relatives want to name your son after you. they hand you a tablet. what do you write?
options: Zachary, after me.
John is his name.
nothing; you hand it back.
fork.reveal: "John is his name." and immediately his mouth was opened, and he spoke, blessing God.

original.note: Greek: rising, dawn, the east; translated dayspring (King James) and Orient (Douay) in Luke 1:78.

trapdoor: what you thought: dayspring is a nice old-fashioned word.
what it means: Christ pictured as sunrise, visiting people who sit in darkness, in the song of a man whose own silence just ended.
what a scholar hears: anatole, the rising of a heavenly light, Latin oriens, hence the Douay's Orient; the same word names the east, where the sun comes up.

446.title: Bethlehem, read slowly (Luke 2:1–20)
446.hook: Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart
446.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 2:1–20 at the Christmas Masses at night and at dawn, sing the angels' words in the Gloria at Sunday Mass, and set up a crèche in homes and churches, a custom often traced to Saint Francis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zachary's tongue was loosed and he sang the Benedictus. Your line was the dayspring from on high. Did you greet the first light? Day four hundred forty-six.

Plastic figures on a lawn. A school play with a kid in a bathrobe. A stable, an innkeeper, an ox and a donkey, a star. So today, try something hard: forget the nativity set, and read only what Luke actually wrote. It's twenty verses. It starts not with angels but with an emperor. A decree goes out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled, and Joseph goes up from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, with Mary, who is with child.
screen: `FORGET THE NATIVITY SET.` → `TWENTY VERSES, READ SLOWLY.` → `IT STARTS WITH AN EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Then one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's all. Notice what isn't there. No innkeeper; Luke never mentions one. No ox and donkey; later tradition brought them in from a line in Isaiah, and Saint Francis had a living ox and donkey beside his crib at Greccio. Even inn may be the wrong picture. Luke's Greek word, kataluma, can mean a guest room, and it's the same word he uses later for the upper room of the Last Supper. So it may have been a crowded family house, with the baby laid where the animals ate. A manger is a feeding trough. And Bethlehem, read as Hebrew, is beit lechem: house of bread. Some Catholic preachers draw a line from there: the child laid in a feeding trough in the house of bread is the one Catholics receive as the bread of life. Then the shepherds, at night, with their flocks. An angel, and their fear, and good news of great joy. And a multitude singing: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." The Gloria at Mass begins with those words. The shepherds go and find it just as they were told, and tell everyone, and everyone wonders. And then the quietest line in the chapter: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Pondering translates a Greek word, symballousa, that pictures putting things together, setting pieces side by side. Luke doesn't say she understood it all. He says she kept it, and turned it over.
screen: `WHAT LUKE DOESN'T SAY.` · `KATALUMA: A GUEST ROOM.` · `A FEEDING TROUGH IN THE HOUSE OF BREAD.` · `GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ponder one thing you've kept. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come up that you haven't figured out yet. Something someone said to you years ago that still comes back. A moment that felt holy and you never told anyone. A hard thing you don't understand. Choose one. Don't solve it. Do what Mary did: hold it, and turn it over, and set it beside other things you know, and see if any piece fits. If you pray, you can ponder it with God. The bell holds the time.
Bethlehem. The city of David, whose name means house of bread, where Mary laid her firstborn son in a manger. Today's word.
Your line: she kept all these things. Today, when something moves you, don't post it or explain it right away. Keep it, and turn it over. Day four hundred forty-six.

original.note: Hebrew: Bethlehem, house of bread, the town of David.

trapdoor: what you thought: the familiar nativity scene.
what it means: a spare account, with no innkeeper or ox, a baby in a feeding trough, shepherds, and a mother who keeps what she can't yet understand.
what a scholar hears: kataluma, a guest room, the word for the upper room in Luke 22:11; symballousa, pondering, putting things together; Bethlehem, house of bread.

447.title: Simeon's song (Luke 2:22–40)
447.hook: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, and a sword for Mary's heart
447.howItsDone: The Church sings the Nunc Dimittis every night at Compline (Night Prayer), keeps the Presentation of the Lord on February 2 with the blessing of candles, and counts Simeon's prophecy as the first of Mary's Seven Sorrows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bethlehem read slowly, with no innkeeper and a manger in the house of bread. Your line was she kept all these things. What did you keep, and turn over? Day four hundred forty-seven.

Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to the Temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked for a firstborn son and a new mother. They bring the offering: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. That detail matters. The law allowed birds in place of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. This is a poor family's offering. And waiting in the Temple courts is an old man named Simeon, just and devout, who had been told by the Holy Ghost that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, UP TO THE TEMPLE.` → `TWO BIRDS: A POOR FAMILY'S OFFERING.` → `AN OLD MAN, WAITING.`

segments.voice: Simeon takes the child up in his arms, blesses God, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; Because my eyes have seen thy salvation." Dismiss is the key word. The Greek, apolueis, is the word for releasing someone: a servant let go from duty, a watchman relieved at the end of the night shift. Simeon has been keeping watch his whole life. Now he's holding what he waited for, and he asks to be let go, in peace. A light, he says, to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. The whole world, and his own people, in one breath. Joseph and Mary are amazed. Then Simeon turns to Mary, and his voice changes. This child is set for the fall and the rising again of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." Catholics count this as the first of the Seven Sorrows of Mary. Right after him comes Anna, a prophetess, very old, a widow who never left the Temple, fasting and praying night and day. She too gives thanks, and speaks of the child to everyone looking for redemption. Two old people, a man and a woman, who waited their whole lives, and both of them recognize a baby. Catholics keep this day on the second of February, called Candlemas because candles are blessed for the light to the Gentiles. And the Church sings Simeon's song every night at Compline, Night Prayer, just before sleep.
screen: `APOLUEIS: A WATCHMAN RELIEVED.` · `A LIGHT TO THE GENTILES.` · `A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.` · `ANNA, WHO NEVER LEFT THE TEMPLE.` · then, large: `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse the end of the day. Settle, and breathe. Imagine it's tonight, and you're about to sleep. Look back over the day, and find one thing your eyes saw that was worth seeing. A face. A kindness. A sky. Hold it the way Simeon held the child. Then let the day go, the way a watchman hands over his post. Tonight, before you sleep, if you pray, you can pray Simeon's own words, the Nunc Dimittis, beginning now thou dost dismiss thy servant. If you don't, just let the day go, in peace. The bell holds the time.
Nunc Dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss, the first words of Simeon's song when he held the child in the Temple, sung every night at Compline. Today's word.
Your line: in peace. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing your eyes saw today, and let the day go. Day four hundred forty-seven.

fork.reveal: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." a watchman asking to be relieved, because what he waited for has come.

original.note: Greek: you release, you let go; in Latin, nunc dimittis, now you dismiss.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man's pious goodbye.
what it means: a lifelong watchman, holding the child he waited for, asking to be relieved of his post in peace; and a warning of a sword for Mary.
what a scholar hears: apolueis, the release of a servant or slave; the birds of Leviticus 12:8 mark a poor family; the song closes the Church's day at Compline.

448.title: He grew (Luke 2:41–52)
448.hook: Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace
448.howItsDone: Catholics pray the finding of Jesus in the Temple as the fifth Joyful Mystery of the rosary, and hear this Gospel on the feast of the Holy Family after Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon held the child and asked to be let go in peace. Your line was in peace. What did your eyes see that was worth seeing? Day four hundred forty-eight, the end of the week.

Every parent's nightmare, in five verses. Every year Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem for the Passover, and when Jesus is twelve they go as usual. The feast ends. They start home in a company of relatives and neighbors, thinking he's somewhere among them. A whole day's walk later, they look for him. He isn't there. They turn back to Jerusalem, and they search. One day. Two days. Luke says it was after three days that they found him.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OLD, AT THE PASSOVER.` → `A DAY'S WALK BEFORE THEY NOTICE.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: He's in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions, and everyone who hears him is astonished at his understanding and his answers. His parents are astonished too, but not in the same way. Mary speaks first, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." And his answer is the first thing Jesus ever says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that you sought me? did you not know, that I must be about my father's business?" The Greek is short and open: literally, in the things of my Father. It could mean my Father's business, or my Father's house. Translations go both ways. And Luke says plainly: they understood not the word. But here's what happens next. He goes down with them to Nazareth, and is subject to them. Obedient. The boy who knows who his Father is goes home and does what his parents say. Then Luke's summary: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." Advanced. Grew. The Greek word for age, helikia, can also mean stature, so the King James says stature, the Douay says age; both are in it. The Church teaches that the Son of God, being truly human, truly grew, in human knowledge as well as in years. Catholics pray this scene as the fifth Joyful Mystery. And after this, Luke says nothing more about him until he is a grown man. That closes this week, and Luke's first two chapters: an orderly account, Zachary's silence, the Ave, the Benedictus, Bethlehem, Simeon, and a boy who grew.
screen: `FOUND AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `MY FATHER'S BUSINESS, OR HOUSE?` · `HE WENT DOWN, AND WAS SUBJECT TO THEM.` · `HELIKIA: AGE, AND STATURE.` · then, large: `JESUS ADVANCED IN WISDOM, AND AGE, AND GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how you've grown. Settle, and breathe. Think back to yourself a year ago, or five years ago. What did you not know then that you know now? Where are you kinder, or braver, or more patient? Take Luke's three words one at a time. Wisdom: something you understand better now. Age: the years themselves, the body that carried you here. Grace: a way you've been given more than you earned. Don't grade yourself. Just notice the growth, even if it's small, even if it came through something hard. If you pray, you can thank God for it. The bell holds the time.
He grew. Luke's words about the boy Jesus after the Temple: he advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men. Today's word.
Your line: growing is holy. Today, tell someone one way you've seen them grow. Day four hundred forty-eight.

fork.setup: you're Mary. after three days of searching, you find your twelve-year-old calmly talking with the teachers in the Temple. what do you say?
options: nothing; you're just relieved.

fork.reveal: "behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." and he answers with a question about his Father's business.

original.note: Greek: age, or stature. Luke 2:52: the Douay says age, the King James says stature.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a precocious boy.
what it means: a frightened search, a boy who knows his Father, an obedient return home, and a Son of God who truly grew.
what a scholar hears: en tois tou patros mou, in the things of my Father, house or business; helikia, age or stature; and Jesus' first words in Luke.
